proposals.relationship: Cooper identifies Genovese’s slavery scholarship as a formative influence on his comparative work on East Africa.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview, 2017 reprint:342 and 348/notes 11, 20, credits the American-South course taught by David Potter and names Genovese among the slavery historians who shaped him. The later French interview, 2022:45–46, calls Genovese the historian who most marked this work, especially plantation production relations and the world economy. The latter witness misdates Roll, Jordan, Roll as 1972; the reprint note 20 and existing publisher record give 1974. No new reading of Genovese’s books, formal mentorship or unqualified adoption of all his interpretations is claimed.

proposals.relationship: Woodward’s history of the post-emancipation American South helped form Cooper’s comparative approach to African slavery.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:341–342 describes Potter’s course and Woodward’s book as part of the education that made Cooper’s dissertation comparative from the start. Note 12 identifies The Origins of the New South, 1877–1913 in a 1971 manifestation. The book is not newly read, and that citation date is not asserted as its first publication. Potter’s teaching remains distinct from Woodward’s reading influence.

proposals.relationship: Cooper names David Brion Davis among the slavery historians who shaped his early scholarship.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:348 explicitly recalls formative slavery scholarship by Genovese, Davis and Emilia Viotti da Costa. Note 21 lists The Problem of Slavery in Western Culture (1966) and The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution (1975). This is Cooper’s retrospective intellectual debt, not proof that both books predated his 1974 dissertation, formal supervision, or fresh reading of either original. Da Costa remains an equally named missing-endpoint lead.

proposals.relationship: Cooper credits sustained reading of Marx with shaping his inquiry into capitalist transformation while testing theory against failed and contested transitions.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:341–344 describes increasing study of Marx, a particular rather than exclusive Marxist thread, and reciprocal testing of theory and historical evidence. Own 2022:46 specifies closer engagement with Capital between his first slavery book and From Slaves to Squatters. The 2000 essay:61–62 and 67/note 3 uses capital as a social relation and the colonial limits of primitive accumulation, citing the Moore/Aveling 1906 volume 1 colonization chapter. These readings retain resistance, contingency and other intellectual sources; the cited Capital edition is not independently reread.

proposals.relationship: Cooper credits collaboration with Stoler for developing a research agenda on colonial societies through the interplay of historical inquiry and anthropology.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:343–344/notes 15–17 explains that similarly framed studies of East African and Sumatran agriculture led to shared conferences, the 1989 American Ethnologist papers and the jointly edited Tensions of Empire (1997). He describes theory and empirical work as mutually informative. Stoler is a collaborator with her own research, not Cooper’s formal teacher, sole origin of colonial studies, or author of every contribution. The 1989 and 1997 introduction bodies and Stoler’s monograph remain unread here; existing source metadata and group route are preserved.

proposals.relationship: Cooper acknowledges learning from Foucault while rejecting the demand that historians all follow a cultural turn.
proposals.evidence_note: Own French interview 2022:47 explicitly says he learned much from reading Foucault, then rejects compulsory disciplinary turns and the neglect of labour history. The witness supports a bounded acknowledged reading resource, with no named Foucault title, exclusive intellectual formation, or acceptance of every Foucauldian claim inferred. The French answers translate English email exchanges and were reviewed by Cooper.

proposals.relationship: Cooper presents Du Bois as a resource for thinking about the changing relationship between social thought, political action and constraint.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview 2022:43–44 corrects the questioners’ suggestion of a continuous early debt: Cooper says full appreciation came years after his first article. He then explains Du Bois’s combination of contextual understanding and transformative action, relating the 1903 colour-line claim to later civil-rights and African-liberation struggles. This is later reflective uptake, not proof that Du Bois directly determined his earliest work or fresh reading of Du Bois’s originals. Historical claims remain Cooper’s.

proposals.relationship: Cooper describes a shared concern with Goody to challenge histories that make Europe the sole driver of the world’s past.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview 2022:56–58, especially 57, responds to the Goody question by identifying a shared criticism of Eurocentric framing. Cooper describes the distinct Burbank–Cooper inter-imperial project, Eurasian focus and tension between comparison and connection. This is an explicitly supported comparison, not a claim of personal contact, causal influence, identical arguments or fresh reading of Goody’s books. Jane Burbank retains equal coauthorship despite lacking a full endpoint.

proposals.relationship: Cooper questions Eley and Nield’s priority for discourse and micropolitics, asking how material structures, long-distance relations and varied political connections also shape class.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000:60–67 praises the joint essay’s conciliatory effort and essential cultural insights while challenging its starting priorities and identity-centred definition of politics. Both Geoff Eley and Keith Nield are targets of one joint argument. Cooper seeks a dynamic relation between discourse and structures, not an economic reversal or dismissal of culture. His Mandela/Buthelezi examples remain his interpretation, not independently checked histories. The original Eley–Nield essay is not freshly read here; their selected joint reply is represented separately.

proposals.relationship: With Nield, Eley answers Cooper that he overstates their differences and leaves the concepts of experience, actual structures and agency insufficiently questioned.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint reply 2000:81–83 quotes Cooper’s political account, agrees on much of his description and on capitalism’s importance, then defends a provisional cultural starting point. The criticism is jointly Eley’s and Keith Nield’s, not sole authorship, and their agreement with Cooper’s concluding historical task is retained. Fresh selected 76–83 reading is distinct from the prior selected 81–86 record. Cooper’s 1995 Thompson essay is invoked by the reply but remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Cooper sees a retrospective categorical difficulty in Thompson’s attempt to show how a working class made itself while assuming the class as its outcome.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000:68/note 11 names The Making of the English Working Class (1963) as a parallel to constructivist arguments that begin from the later category and miss alternative affinities. This is a precise qualification, alongside the positive analogy to struggles against class formation at 62. It is not a wholesale rejection of Thompson, a fresh reading of The Making, or reuse of the separately unread 1995 retrospective.

proposals.relationship: Cooper uses Chakrabarty’s distinction between abstract and real labour to analyze the continuing tension between general claims and workers’ particularity.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000:62 and 67–68/note 4 explicitly takes up Chakrabarty’s distinction, naming Marx After Marxism: History, Subalternity and Difference (Meanjin 52, 1993:421–434). Cooper emphasizes that both general and specific registers can be useful in labour politics. This is a stated conceptual resource rather than agreement with every Chakrabarty argument or fresh reading of the 1993 original. It is distinct from the existing group account and from the 1989 Bengal book.

proposals.relationship: Cooper uses James’s account of exploitation and transatlantic revolutionary mobilization to connect labour organization with political ideas across empires.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000:63/note 7 at 68 attributes to James both the organization of Caribbean plantation labour and the movement of revolutionary news and claims. The note cites The Black Jacobins in its 1963 edition while the prose dates the original argument 1938. Cooper places Trouillot’s qualification beside James’s account; this is an argumentative use, not fresh reading or independent verification of James’s historical claims.

proposals.relationship: Cooper uses Trouillot’s account of varied Haitian political imaginations to qualify a wholly Jacobin account of the revolution.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000:63/note 7 at 68 explicitly contrasts the Jacobin current with other imaginations brought from Africa and redeployed in Haiti. James’s transatlantic account remains positively represented alongside this qualification. The note points to Trouillot’s 1995 book; the citation’s title wording is not taken as an alternative work. No fresh book reading or verification of every Haitian case is claimed.

proposals.relationship: Cooper positively uses Eley and Blackbourn’s account of varied capitalist transitions alongside his criticism of Eley and Nield’s later class framework.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000:62 praises Eley’s argument that non-English histories are particular processes of accumulation rather than failed copies of England. Note 3 at 67 identifies the jointly authored The Peculiarities of German History (1984). David Blackbourn retains coauthor credit; the prose’s specific praise of Eley does not remove Blackbourn’s joint authorship. The book is unread here, and this particular resource neither erases the reciprocal 2000 critique nor establishes wholesale personal formation.
